title: Opponents and neighbors
hook: Hasidism met fierce opposition from the Vilna Gaon's circle; today both ways of life thrive

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Maggid's circle carried Hasidism across Eastern Europe. Your line was pass it on. Did you share one thing you've learned? Today, the people who pushed back. Day three hundred twelve.

Every family has its big argument. The one about how things should be done. How holidays work. What really matters. Voices get raised, doors get slammed, and for a while it seems like there's no way back. For a few weeks now we've been hearing Hasidic stories. But Hasidism didn't spread without a fight. Some leading rabbis of the time thought it was a dangerous mistake, and said so, loudly. Today: the opponents, and what happened to the argument. Today's word: Mitnagdim.
screen: `EVERY FAMILY'S BIG ARGUMENT.` → `HASIDISM DIDN'T SPREAD QUIETLY.` → `THE OPPONENTS.`

segments.voice: Mitnagdim means opponents, the ones who stood against. Their leading figure was Rabbi Elijah of Vilna, called the Vilna Gaon, the genius of Vilna. He and his circle were alarmed by the new movement. The Hasidim changed the prayer book and prayed at their own times. They put enormous weight on the rebbe. Some were accused of neglecting deep Talmud study for joy and song. For communities still shaken by the false messiahs of earlier generations, it looked risky. The community of Vilna declared a ban against the Hasidim. The conflict was bitter. There were bans on both sides, harsh words, even denunciations to the government. It's not a pretty chapter. The tradition says Shneur Zalman once came to Vilna hoping to make peace, and the Gaon would not see him. But here's the rest of the story. The argument changed both sides. The Gaon's student, Chaim of Volozhin, founded a great yeshiva, and his teaching stressed Torah study as the heart of Jewish life. And Hasidism, for its part, held on to both its warmth and its learning. Later, as modern times brought new challenges, the two camps often found themselves on the same side. Today, the Hasidic world and the yeshiva world, sometimes called Litvish, from Lithuania, both flourish, often on the same streets. The Talmud tells of a heavenly voice that settled an old dispute between the schools of Hillel and Shammai: these and these are the words of the living God. Two paths. Both endure.
screen: `MITNAGDIM: THE OPPONENTS.` · `THE VILNA GAON.` · `VILNA'S BITTER BAN.` · `THESE AND THESE.` · then, large: `BOTH PATHS ENDURE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: respect a rival school. Settle, and breathe. Think of a group whose way of doing things rubs you the wrong way. Another team, another school, another style of doing what you do. Not an enemy. A rival. Now ask one honest question: what do they protect that I might forget? What do they get right? You don't have to agree with them. Just find the one true thing in their way. If you pray, you can pray for them. The bell holds the time.
Mitnagdim. The opponents of early Hasidism, led by the Vilna Gaon. The argument was bitter; today both ways of life thrive side by side.
Your line: both paths endure. Today, when you hear yourself dismissing people who do things differently, name one thing they do well. Day three hundred twelve.

howItsDone: Today Hasidic communities and the Lithuanian-style yeshiva world live side by side in places like Jerusalem, Bnei Brak and Brooklyn, each with its own customs, and study many of the same texts.

original.note: Hebrew: opponents, those who stand against. The name stuck to the Vilna Gaon's circle.

trapdoor: what you thought: the bad guys in the Hasidic story.
what it means: serious scholars who feared the new movement, in a bitter argument that both sides survived.

what a scholar hears: the opposition shaped both camps: the Volozhin yeshiva and Nefesh HaChaim on one side, Hasidic courts with strong study traditions of their own on the other, and later a shared front toward modernity.

notes: This is a sensitive history for both communities. Please check that neither side is caricatured and that the grievances listed (changes to prayer, the role of the rebbe, alleged neglect of study, fear after Sabbateanism) are fairly stated.

The Vilna ban of 1772 and later bans (1781, 1796–97) and denunciations to Russian authorities (1798–1800, including Shneur Zalman's arrest): the script mentions denunciations only in general terms. Confirm.
The tradition that Shneur Zalman (with Menachem Mendel of Vitebsk) sought to meet the Gaon and was refused: confirm.
Volozhin yeshiva founded 1803 by Chaim of Volozhin: only named, not dated, in the voice.
Eruvin 13b ('these and these are the words of the living God') paraphrased; used about Hillel and Shammai, applied here by analogy.

Editor review (2026-10-01): fairness fix: 'Hasidism, in turn, took learning seriously, too' and the trapdoor's 'a more learned Hasidism' implied Hasidim had not valued study; reworded. Cut superlatives about the Gaon and 'the greatest rabbis', uncited dates (1772, 1803, 'a century earlier', 'by the eighteen hundreds') from voice, screen and games, 'nobody tells it as one', and the wrong 'two weeks'. Eruvin 13b now framed as the heavenly voice.
